question:
A 31-year-old male is brought to the emergency department by ambulance due to altered mental status
and persistent seizure activity. He had been drinking alcohol with friends for several hours when they
noticed his absence. He was found unresponsive, lying prone in the backyard surrounded by vomit.
Despite receiving two doses of intravenous lorazepam, his tonic extension and rhythmic jerking of the
limbs have continued. His finger-stick glucose is normal. Vital signs include a temperature of 37.2°C
(99°F), pulse of 84/min, respirations of 18/min, blood pressure of 120/80, and oxygen saturation of 85%
on room air. On examination, his eyes are open and deviated upward, he is unresponsive to verbal or
painful stimuli, and pulmonary findings include decreased breath sounds and crackles throughout. His
upper extremities are flexed, and his lower extremities are extended with rhythmic jerking in both. After
receiving a bolus of levetiracetam, which of the following tests is most likely to confirm the underlying
cause of his seizure activity? Answer Choices: (A) Serum electrolyte panel (B) Computerized
tomography (CT) of the head with contrast (C) Serum ammonia level (D) Non-contrast computed
tomography (CT) of the head (E) Lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid analysis (F)
Electroencephalography (EEG) (G) Arterial blood gas analysis (H) Brain magnetic resonance imaging
(MRI) without contrast (I) Chest radiography (J) Urine toxicology screen

A. Computerized tomography (CT) of the head with contrast
B. Serum electrolyte panel
C. Chest radiography
D. Arterial blood gas analysis
E. Serum ammonia level
F. Electroencephalography (EEG)
G. Lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid analysis
H. Non-contrast computed tomography (CT) of the head
I. Urine toxicology screen
J. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) without contrast
